summary: Evaluates five candidate protocols for the IPFIX flow export protocol against the requirements the IPFIX working group produced. It groups the candidates, scores them, and recommends choosing NetFlow v9 as the basis for IPFIX.

eli5.summary: Five contestants try out for a job. The judges compare them with a checklist and pick the one called NetFlow v9.

subtitle: Five candidate protocols for flow export are compared, and NetFlow v9 is recommended as the starting point.

tldr.problem: The IPFIX working group had to choose a protocol for exporting flow information from routers and probes, and five different candidates had been submitted.
tldr.mechanism: An evaluation team compared the candidates against the working group's requirements document, grouping them by design goals, data representation and protocol flow, and then checking item by item.
tldr.outcome: The team recommended starting from NetFlow v9 because it is the simplest protocol meeting a large share of the requirements, while adding transport, security and reliability mechanisms.

today: RFC 3955 is an Informational RFC, published in October 2004, with no obsoleting or updating RFC in the metadata. It records why NetFlow v9, documented in RFC 3954, was recommended as the basis for IPFIX, measured against RFC 3917.

sections.title: The Evaluation Task
sections.content:
The IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) working group was chartered to select a protocol for exporting flow information from traffic-observing devices such as routers or dedicated probes. An evaluation team was formed, and each submitted protocol had an advocate who wrote an evaluation of it against the requirements document, RFC 3917.

Five candidates were evaluated: CRANE, Diameter, LFAP, NetFlow v9 and Streaming IPDR. This document evaluates them against the requirements and, more generally, against the working group charter.
sections.eli5: A group needed to pick one way for network gadgets to report traffic. Five ideas were offered, so a team compared them.

sections.title: The Five Candidates
sections.content:
CRANE carries accounting information from network elements to mediation and business support systems, over a reliable protocol such as TCP or, preferably, SCTP, with application-layer acknowledgements and templates. Diameter is an evolution of RADIUS for authentication, authorization and accounting, and conveys data as attribute/value pairs over TCP or, preferably, SCTP.

LFAP began as the Lightweight Flow Admission Protocol and later became the Lightweight Flow Accounting Protocol. It runs over TCP and reports each flow with a Flow Accounting Request when a flow is identified and Flow Update Notification messages later. NetFlow v9 is a generalized version of Cisco's NetFlow; the exporter sends template, options and data FlowSets to the collector. It is the only candidate that works over UDP. Streaming IPDR runs over TCP and uses XML-Schema-based descriptions, with data in XML or in the XDR encoding.
sections.eli5: The five contestants are built for different jobs. Some were made for billing, one for logging in, and one only for sending traffic counts quickly.

sections.title: Grouping the Candidates
sections.content:
By design goal, NetFlow and LFAP aim at high-performance flow metering; IPDR and CRANE at carrier-grade multi-purpose accounting; and Diameter at general-purpose AAA. By data representation, CRANE, IPDR and NetFlow use an external description such as templates, which allows very compact encoding, while Diameter and LFAP use Type/Length/Value encodings that can be partly decoded without context but take more space and bandwidth.

By protocol flow, IPDR and NetFlow are mainly unidirectional from exporter to collector. CRANE and LFAP are bidirectional and negotiate templates or data. Diameter negotiates capabilities and is then essentially unidirectional.
sections.eli5: Some contestants send a short note with a legend, some stuff every item with its own label, and some chat back and forth first. Each style has costs.

sections.title: Item-by-Item Comparison
sections.content:
Several findings stand out. On metering reliability, LFAP alone explicitly handles the possibility that data is lost in the metering process. On sampling, CRANE and IPDR do not mention it, LFAP does not support it, and NetFlow v9 does. On timestamps, all protocols meet the required one-centisecond precision, but NetFlow reports times relative to sysUpTime, and its one-second UNIX Secs field cannot synchronize with UTC without losing precision.

For congestion awareness, all candidates except NetFlow v9 run over a single TCP or SCTP connection; NetFlow v9 was defined for UDP, and a separate document describes running it over SCTP. NetFlow v9 is the only protocol where a reliable transport is optional and the only one without application-level acknowledgements. For security, all can use lower-layer IPsec or TLS, and the author doubts that built-in security in Diameter or LFAP adds enough to justify the complexity. Only LFAP has a pull-like inquiry; none of the candidates includes explicit anonymization support.
sections.eli5: The judges checked each rule on the list. Every contestant passed some and missed others; NetFlow was simplest but did not promise safe, reliable delivery.

sections.title: Conclusion and Recommendation
sections.content:
If the aim were a carrier-grade accounting protocol, CRANE, Diameter or Streaming IPDR would probably be chosen. But the goal was to standardize existing practice, and earlier NetFlow versions were widely implemented and used. The report credits Cisco's strong position in the router market but also the value of a simple protocol that does one thing well; writing a collector only requires receiving data.

The team's opinion is that the charter is best served by starting with NetFlow v9 and working on the lacking mechanisms for transport, security, reliability and redundant configurations, carefully, to keep simplicity. NetFlow v9 as evaluated specifies no security mechanisms, and its other major gap is a congestion-aware transport, such as TCP or (PR-)SCTP. LFAP was judged to carry baggage from its origins as a flow admission protocol. For the NetFlow v9 specification itself, see RFC 3954.
sections.eli5: The judges chose the simplest contestant and said, now teach it to travel safely and politely, but do not make it complicated.
